analysis.one_liner: Caps fossil carbon sold in America, bans financial speculation in the permits, and pays every resident a monthly dividend.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 11, 2009 by a Democratic senator with one Republican cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The CLEAR Act would have limited the total amount of fossil carbon (coal, oil, natural gas) allowed into the U.S. economy, shrinking the cap each year. Fuel producers and importers would buy permits at monthly government auctions, with prices kept between a floor and a ceiling. Three-quarters of the auction money would go back to every person lawfully living in the United States as a monthly, tax-free "energy security dividend" designed to more than cover the higher fuel prices; the rest would fund clean energy, worker transition aid, and help for low-income households. The bill also barred fuel companies from creating or trading derivatives on the permits, keeping Wall Street out of the carbon market.
analysis.who_benefits: Every individual lawfully residing in the United States would receive a monthly, tax-free energy security dividend equal to a per-person share of three-quarters of the permit auction proceeds. Low-income families would get additional help: utility-bill assistance, weatherization, home-heating-oil conversion, and matching grants for efficiency loans, and could borrow against future dividends to invest in energy efficiency. Coal workers and communities hit hardest by the transition would get targeted aid and retraining. Energy consumers would gain a new Treasury Office of Consumer Advocacy, and clean energy industries would gain a dedicated trust fund for loans, grants, and research.

how_it_helps.text: Three-quarters of all permit auction proceeds would be deposited in a Carbon Refund Trust Fund and paid out as monthly, tax-free energy security dividends to every lawful U.S. resident.

The remaining quarter of auction proceeds, plus penalties and import fees, would fund a Clean Energy Reinvestment Trust Fund covering worker and community transition assistance, worker retraining, low-income utility-bill aid, weatherization, residential fuel switching, and clean energy research and deployment.

Fuel producers and importers would be the only bidders allowed at the auctions, and they would be banned from creating, buying, selling, or trading carbon share derivatives, with regulators directed to prohibit fraud, manipulation, and excessive speculation.

The bill would establish an Office of Consumer Advocacy in the Treasury to represent residential and small-commercial energy customers, monitor complaints, and investigate how the program affects utility rates.
The bill would set binding emission targets: greenhouse gas emissions no more than 80% of 2005 levels by 2020 and no more than 17% of 2005 levels by 2050.
Individuals could borrow against their future dividends to pay for energy-efficiency and clean-energy upgrades that would lower their bills, and companies could not hoard permits to speculate.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers and importers would pay for a permit for every ton of coal, oil, and gas they sell into the U.S. market, and those costs would be passed into fuel and electricity prices. Households that use much more energy than average (for example, long-distance drivers or homes with poor insulation before weatherization) could pay more in higher prices than they receive in dividends. Financial firms would lose the chance to build a carbon derivatives trading business, which the bill deliberately closed off.

drawbacks.text: The permit price would be capped by a "safety valve": in 2012 no permit could cost more than $21 per ton of carbon dioxide equivalent, and if the price hit the ceiling the government would sell extra permits beyond the cap, which weakens the guarantee that emissions actually fall.
Higher fuel prices would not evenly offset every household's dividend; heavy energy users could come out behind, at least until efficiency investments lowered their bills.

The cap would barely decline at first: the quantity of carbon shares would hold at the 2012 level through 2014, then fall only 0.25% in 2015, with the reduction rate rising a further 0.25% per year thereafter.
The bill would count voluntary carbon-reduction purchases against the cap, a mechanism critics of offset systems have said can overstate real emission cuts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is unusually weighted toward ordinary households: all permits are auctioned (rather than given free to polluters), most of the money is returned per person, and derivatives trading is prohibited from the start. The main honest objections are the weak early cap, the safety valve that can let emissions exceed the limit if prices spike, and transition costs for households and regions dependent on cheap fossil energy, which the bill partially funds through its transition-assistance provisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the CLEAR Act on December 11, 2009, for herself and Senator Susan Collins.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and importers never had to buy a permit for the carbon they sell, and financial firms were never shut out of or disciplined in a carbon market, because the bill never advanced. No carbon limits, consumer dividends, or anti-speculation rules were enacted at all.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and carbon traders

for.name: Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CLEAR Act on December 11, 2009 and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor, making the bill a bipartisan introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 11, 2009 and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Democrat (Cantwell) and a Republican (Collins) — but because it never reached a hearing or a vote, the chamber's partisan split on it was never tested.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and gas producers and importers
industries.note: They would have had to buy a declining-supply permit for every ton of fossil carbon sold into the U.S. market, with a five-times-price penalty for noncompliance. Keeping the bill from advancing meant those costs never arrived.

industries.industry: Wall Street and financial trading firms
industries.note: The bill would have allowed only fuel producers and importers to buy permits and banned anyone from creating or trading carbon permit derivatives, foreclosing an entirely new trading market. Its defeat preserved the possibility of that market and avoided any speculation limits.
A quarter of auction proceeds would have flowed through a dedicated trust fund for clean energy loans, grants, research, weatherization, and worker retraining — demand the industry never received.

They would have faced higher fuel input costs, but the bill pairs border fees on imports from countries without carbon limits with targeted relief funds for industries that could not compete, softening the hit.
